articles.title: Identity theft protection is changing: What to look for
articles.summary: Identity theft now includes account takeover, phone hijacking and payment card exposure. Here's what to look for in identity theft protection services.
articles.body: For years, many people thought of identity theft as a specific event. Someone opens a credit card in your name, runs up a balance and leaves you to clean up the damage. That still happens, but identity theft has become more complicated. Criminals may take over an existing bank account instead of opening a new one. They may transfer your phone number to another device or expose your payment-card information. They may also use your personal details in a convincing scam or combine information from several breaches to impersonate you. Your identity may be connected to your bank, credit cards, retirement accounts and phone service. It can also connect to medical providers, social media profiles, shopping accounts and information collected by data brokers. That broader risk changes what you should look for in identity theft protection. A useful service should do more than alert you that something may be wrong. It should help you understand what happened, decide what to do next and find support when the situation becomes difficult to resolve. Here's what you can do now to protect yourself, what to look for in an identity theft protection service and where extra monitoring and recovery support may help. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com SIM SWAP SCAM DRAINED FLORIDA WOMAN'S BANK ACCOUNT IN MINUTES Identity theft now includes account takeover New-account fraud remains a concern, but account takeover can be just as disruptive. In an account takeover, a criminal gains access to an account you already own. They may change the password, replace the recovery email address, add a new phone number or make unauthorized purchases and transfers. The warning signs can be easy to miss. You might receive a password-reset alert you did not request, notice that your phone suddenly loses service or see a small unfamiliar charge on a credit card. Other warning signs include unexpected changes to your account profile, a new device connected to your email account or a notification about a transaction you do not recognize. Scams have also become more personalized. A criminal may know your name, location, family details or the name of your bank before contacting you. As a result, a fake text, phone call or email can seem much more convincing. Identity protection has expanded beyond traditional credit monitoring. Today, you may also want help watching financial accounts, payment activity, phone changes, exposed personal information and suspicious transactions. What to look for in an identity theft protection service The best service depends on your financial life and comfort level. However, several questions are worth asking before you sign up. 1) What does it actually monitor? Start with coverage. Does the service monitor only your credit file? Does it also watch bank accounts, credit cards, investments, retirement accounts and phone takeovers? What about data breaches, home titles or personal information appearing in risky locations? No service can monitor everything. Extra coverage offers little value if you do not use the accounts or features involved. The important question is whether the service watches the areas where you are most likely to face risk. 2) How useful are the alerts? An alert only helps when you understand what it means and what to do next. Look for alerts that explain the activity clearly. A notification about a new credit inquiry, suspicious charge or account change should help you decide whether the activity is legitimate or requires action. You should also be able to receive alerts through channels you regularly check, such as email, text message, phone or a mobile app. Remember, an alert is a prompt to investigate rather than proof that fraud occurred. A legitimate purchase may look unusual because of a merchant's billing name, travel, a family member's activity or a recurring subscription. 3) Does the service offer recovery support? Monitoring can tell you that something may be wrong. Recovery is the work that follows. If identity theft occurs, you may need to contact banks, credit bureaus, government agencies, phone providers and other companies. You may also have to dispute fraudulent accounts, replace compromised credentials, document phone calls and keep track of multiple case numbers. That process can become overwhelming, particularly when several accounts are involved. Look for a service that provides access to people who can help explain the recovery process and organize the next steps. A restoration specialist may not be able to make every decision for you. You may still need to provide documents or speak directly with your bank. However, knowledgeable support can make the process less confusing. 4) Are reimbursement benefits clearly explained? Some identity protection services include reimbursement or expense coverage for certain eligible losses. Review what the coverage applies to and how much is available. Then check what documentation you need. Also see whether separate terms apply to identity theft, stolen funds, scams, legal expenses or professional assistance. Pay close attention to eligibility requirements, exclusions, geographic limitations and the difference between "up to" amounts and guaranteed payments. 5) Does the plan fit your situation? A person with one checking account and a single credit card may need a different level of monitoring than someone managing multiple bank accounts, investments, retirement savings and property. Families and caregivers may also value phone support and recovery assistance, especially when helping an older relative navigate a complicated identity issue. Before enrolling, compare the plan's features with protections you already receive through your bank, credit-card company, employer or another service. DIY IDENTITY PROTECTION VS PAID SERVICES: WHAT WORKS IN 2026 Monitoring and recovery serve different purposes Monitoring and recovery address two different parts of an identity theft problem. Monitoring looks for warning signs such as a new credit inquiry, suspicious financial activity, a possible breach, an unusual charge or personal information appearing in a monitored location. Recovery begins after something has gone wrong. It may involve contacting banks, disputing accounts, replacing identification, filing reports, documenting calls and following up with multiple organizations. That is why recovery support deserves as much attention as the list of things a service monitors. An alert may tell you there is a problem. The harder part can be figuring out how to fix it. What you should do yourself to protect your identity Before paying for additional protection, there are several steps you can take yourself to make fraud harder and catch suspicious activity sooner. Check your credit reports Review all three credit reports for unfamiliar accounts, inquiries and addresses. If something looks wrong, investigate it quickly instead of waiting for another warning sign. You can access your reports and look for accounts you do not recognize, credit inquiries you did not authorize or personal information that appears incorrect. Turn on account alerts Enable transaction, password-change and login alerts through your banks, credit-card companies and other important accounts. These notifications can help you spot suspicious activity sooner. Pay particular attention to alerts about password resets, new devices, changes to contact information and money transfers. Strengthen your passwords and account security Use strong, unique passwords for important accounts and turn on multifactor authentication whenever it is available. Secure your primary email account first. If a criminal gains access to your email, they may be able to reset passwords for banking, shopping and other accounts connected to it. Freeze your credit when appropriate A credit freeze can make it harder for someone to open a new account using your identity. You can freeze and unfreeze your credit directly with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Remember that a credit freeze focuses on new-account fraud. It does not stop a criminal from taking over an account you already have. Slow down when a message or call feels urgent Be cautious with unexpected calls, texts, emails and payment requests. Scammers often create urgency because they want you to act before you have time to question what they are telling you. Instead of responding through the message you received, contact the company through its official website, app or phone number. Keep records if something goes wrong Save screenshots, case numbers, reports and notes from conversations involving suspicious activity. Good records can make it easier to work with banks, credit bureaus, phone providers and other organizations during the recovery process. These steps can reduce your risk and help you catch problems sooner. However, some people may want additional monitoring and hands-on recovery assistance. That raises another question: What should you actually look for in an identity theft protection service? What broader identity theft protection can offer Even with good security habits, identity theft can still happen. Your Social Security number, financial information or other personal data may already be exposed without you knowing it. That is where an identity theft protection service may add another layer of help. Depending on the service and plan, protection can include credit monitoring, financial account monitoring, alerts about suspicious activity and assistance if your identity is compromised. When comparing services, look beyond how many things they claim to monitor. Pay attention to how quickly alerts arrive, what help you receive after a problem occurs and whether reimbursement benefits come with limits or exclusions. Identity theft protection features worth looking for Newer identity theft protection services increasingly focus on risks that go beyond someone opening a new credit account in your name. Payment card exposure monitoring Some services can alert you when payment-card information may have appeared in a breach or other risky location. That can give you a reason to review the card, update payment information or contact the issuer. It does not replace checking your statements or reporting unauthorized charges, but it can provide another warning that your information may be exposed. Unexpected and suspicious charge alerts Some identity protection services can flag transactions that appear unusual or deserve a closer look. That can be useful when criminals test an account with a small purchase or when activity falls outside your typical spending pattern. An alert does not automatically mean fraud occurred, so always verify suspicious transactions through your bank or card issuer's official app, website or phone number. Scam support and reimbursement benefits Scams can move quickly, especially when criminals create urgency or impersonate someone you trust. Some identity protection plans provide guidance when you are unsure whether something is a scam and may include reimbursement for certain eligible scam-related or identity theft losses. Before choosing a plan, review what qualifies for reimbursement, how much coverage is available, what documentation you need and which exclusions apply. Around-the-clock identity assistance Some services offer access to advisors or support teams when you receive a suspicious message, notice an unfamiliar transaction or have another identity concern. Having someone available to explain your options can be especially useful when you are unsure what to do first. Identity restoration support Recovery assistance can become one of the most valuable parts of an identity protection service after fraud occurs. A restoration specialist may help you understand which organizations to contact, what documentation to gather and how to work through problems involving banks, credit bureaus, phone providers and other companies. When comparing identity theft protection services, look at both how well the service can warn you about potential trouble and how much help it provides once something has already gone wrong. Criminals can target accounts you already have, your phone number, payment cards, retirement savings and personal information. That means identity theft protection should match the financial and digital accounts you actually use. Start with the protections you can control yourself. Review your credit reports, turn on account alerts, strengthen your passwords, use multifactor authentication and consider freezing your credit. Then, if you want additional monitoring and recovery assistance, compare services based on what they actually watch and what happens when something goes wrong. Look for broader monitoring, scam support and identity restoration assistance that fit your needs. Still, no identity protection service can replace careful account security and regular financial reviews. What worries you most about identity theft today: someone opening a new account in your name, taking over an account you already have or using your personal information to scam you? articles.title: A Harvard Economist Says the Debt Reckoning Is Coming and Names Who Pays for It
articles.summary: Harvard economist Kenneth Rogoff left Jackson Hole with a specific warning about who absorbs the cost when America's debt reckoning finally arrives, and the...
articles.body:
Rogoff warns a U.S. debt crisis is coming, driven by a deficit running at 6 to 7% of GDP with no political coalition willing to close it.

Rogoff explicitly names higher earners as the ones who pay, pointing to relatively low U.S. taxes and unadjusted retirement ages as the likeliest fiscal levers.

Roth accounts and TIPS beat traditional bonds and 401(k)s if repression takes hold, since the 30-year Treasury at 5.2% can be eroded by inflation.

Kenneth Rogoff, the Harvard economics professor and former chief economist at the International Monetary Fund, spoke with CNBC from Jackson Hole on August 28, 2026. He was direct about where he thinks the country is headed.

He told viewers, "I think we will have some kind of debt crisis, financial repression, inflation, maybe something more dramatic. We might not be the only ones the U.K., France, Belgium. But yeah, I think it's coming not because it has to happen, but that's true about every debt crisis."

Rogoff says the deficit is running at 6% to 7% of GDP during peacetime, and no political coalition is preparing to close it. If he is right, the adjustment eventually lands somewhere.

He named a direction: "The lower income people don't have anything to worry about. And the higher income people added to your tax bill."

If you are near retirement, in it, or a high earner planning for one, it matters whether you build the next decade around today's tax code and today's real yields, or around what Rogoff is describing.

Rogoff is describing a slow political failure that ends with a bill, and he is unusually specific about whose bill it is.

He put the problem inside the country. "I mean, the biggest threat over, say, the next 5 to 10 years is from the inside, that we just aren't prepared to balance our budget. We're rich. We were always rich. We could afford to."

articles.title: Alt-right troll Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported
articles.summary: The controversial Gamergate figure Milo Yiannopoulos has been sent back to the UK by ICE after overstaying his visa.
articles.body: Alt-right troll Milo Yiannopoulos was arrested by ICE on Thursday, and today the Department of Homeland Security confirmed to Reuters and the Washington Post that he had been deported to the UK. Yiannopoulos came to the US legally in 2019, but overstayed his visa. After he failed to appear in court for an immigration hearing, a final order of removal was issued ​on July 22. The British national made a name for himself as an editor at Steve Bannon’s Breitbart and an early supporter of Donald Trump’s. He has had a long history of controversial statements and associations, including reportedly helping arrange Trump’s dinner with Kanye West and white nationalist Nick Fuentes, and he was a key figure in the online harassment campaign Gamergate. In recent years, however, his antics have led to a falling out with most significant figures on the right, including MAGA influencer Laura Loomer. He has denied condoning statutory rape or pedophilia, but he has suggested it’s acceptable for an adult to have a sexual relationship with a 13-year-old. There’s no word if the 44 interns in a trenchcoat who also constitute the entity known as Milo Yiannopoulos have also been deported.

articles.title: Furto de energia: Santos, São Vicente e Praia Grande somam 873 casos | G1
articles.standfirst: Levantamento da CPFL Piratininga reúne irregularidades identificadas entre janeiro e junho de 2026. Praia Grande concentrou mais de 70% dos casos.
articles.summary: O furto de energia na Baixada Santista resultou na recuperação de 1,5 milhão de kWh pela CPFL, volume que abasteceria centenas de residências por um ano.
articles.body:
CPFL aponta levantamento de furtos de energia nas cidades da Baixada Santista. — Foto: Divulgação CPFL Energia

A CPFL Piratininga identificou 873 irregularidades no consumo de energia em Santos , São Vicente e Praia Grande , no litoral de São Paulo, entre janeiro e junho de 2026. Segundo a concessionária, as fiscalizações permitiram recuperar 1,5 milhão de kWh.

Praia Grande concentrou a maior parte dos casos, com 624 ocorrências, o equivalente a mais de 70% do total. São Vicente teve 166 irregularidades, enquanto Santos registrou outras 83.

De acordo com a CPFL, os casos foram identificados por meio de inspeções, análises técnicas, denúncias de moradores e, quando necessário, operações realizadas em parceria com autoridades policiais.

Entre as irregularidades encontradas estão as ligações clandestinas, conhecidas como “gatos”, adulterações de medidores e outras intervenções feitas para reduzir ou impedir o registro correto do consumo de energia.

Segundo a concessionária, essas práticas podem provocar sobrecarga na rede elétrica, oscilações e interrupções no fornecimento, além de aumentar o risco de curto-circuito, incêndio e choque elétrico.

A CPFL informou ainda que o combate às irregularidades ajuda a reduzir as perdas de energia consideradas nos processos de revisão tarifária da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel).

O Código Penal equipara a energia elétrica a uma coisa móvel para fins do crime de furto. Desde maio deste ano, a pena prevista para o furto simples passou de um a quatro anos para um a seis anos de reclusão, além de multa, após a entrada em vigor da Lei nº 15.397/2026.

Denúncias de possíveis irregularidades podem ser feitas de forma anônima pelos canais de atendimento da CPFL, pelo aplicativo CPFL Energia ou pelo site da concessionária.

A empresa também utiliza sistemas de monitoramento, medidores protegidos e tecnologias de acompanhamento remoto para direcionar as fiscalizações.

articles.title: GOP gambles on midterm dividends from RFK Jr.’s MAHA
articles.summary: Less than three months ahead of the midterm elections, the main political organization supporting Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement has barely made a splash to help boost Republican candidates. President Trump and parts of the Republican Party have aligned his Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement with MAHA and Kennedy,…
articles.body:
Less than three months ahead of the midterm elections, the main political organization supporting Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement has barely made a splash to help boost Republican candidates.

President Trump and parts of the Republican Party have aligned his Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement with MAHA and Kennedy, hoping to recapture a key piece of the broad coalition that helped Trump win the White House in 2024.

MAHA helped give Trump an important ally in Kennedy, a longtime Democrat before he endorsed Trump and joined his administration. That gave Republicans access to a new group of voters, which could be key to helping lift the party in a year where Trump’s ratings are underwater.

MAHA’s political leaders, most notably Kennedy ally Tony Lyons, have been working to show the White House that its MAHA outreach will pay dividends. If the MAHA coalition can be counted on as a reliable conservative voting bloc in November and keep Republicans in power, Trump would be able to prioritize more of Kennedy’s agenda.

Lyons runs the MAHA PAC, the primary political operation behind the MAHA movement, as well as its affiliated super PAC, MAHA Action. In March, he launched a $100 million fundraising campaign to elect MAHA-aligned, Trump-endorsed GOP candidates.

It was an ambitious undertaking. In the first half of 2025, prior to the Lyons pledge, the committee spent $3.8 million, and none if it went to candidates.

To date, MAHA PAC has raised about $2.4 million and has only about $287,000 cash on hand, according to the most recent campaign finance filings.

Lyons did not respond to a request for comment from The Hill.

Most of the contributions to the PAC are small-dollar amounts from individual donors. To date in 2026, MAHA PAC has received over $1 million from just four donors.

Venni Capital, a New York investment firm linked to a generic drug manufacturer, gave two $50,000 donations.

Botanic Tonics, a kratom and kava beverage company, donated a total of $1 million to the PAC. According to reporting by the New York Times, Kennedy tried to discourage Ohio’s governor from moving forward with a crackdown on kratom products.

In addition, the Times found Homeland Security Sec. Markwayne Mullin holds a financial stake in the company that’s worth as much as $1 million.

Mark Mikhael, the CEO of a drug compounding company called Olympia Pharmaceuticals, donated $25,000. Mikhael joined the board of MAHA PAC in 2025.

And while MAHA PAC and MAHA Action have endorsed a slate of GOP candidates for Congress and in the states, barely any money has reached them.

The MAHA brand is strong, but the political organization has seemingly been unable to leverage that support into a significant financial machine for Republicans.

“MAHA doesn’t function best lining up with one political party over another,” said GOP strategist Liz Mair. “When I look at spread of incumbents who are interesting to MAHA voters, it’s not 100 percent Republicans.”

Jeff Hutt, who worked on Kennedy’s presidential campaign and was formerly involved with the PAC, said the small dollar donors were the heart and soul of Kennedy’s campaign. They were not necessarily Trump supporters or even Republicans.

But when Kennedy dropped out of the race and endorsed Trump, those voters listened.

“They believed in Bobby Kennedy and they believed in what he was doing. But you take Bobby Kennedy out of that equation, and you just put it on a select group of Republicans who are running under the MAHA title, I just don’t think the interest is really there,” Hutt said.

In races for House and Senate, MAHA groups have endorsed incumbent Republican Reps. Tom Barrett (Mich.), Julia Letlow (La.), and Scott Perry (Pa.), as well as Michael Alfonso in Wisconsin, Austin Rogers in Florida, and Brandon Herrera in Texas.

Perry and Barrett are considered battleground candidates, while Alfonso, Rogers and Herrera are pursuing solidly Republican House seats where the incumbent isn’t seeking reelection.

Letlow’s primary against Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) was one of the only campaigns MAHA PAC has spent substantial money, although the $700,000 was still short of the $1 million they pledged to spend.

Letlow also received Trump’s endorsement over fellow Republican and former Rep. John Fleming.

“MAHA PAC promised $100 million to help Republican candidates and has been practically nonexistent. The rest of the Republican coalition is working overtime to hold the House and Senate, but where is MAHA PAC?” said one GOP operative involved in the midterms. “They talked a big game, candidates aligned with them in good faith, and now three months out, they’ve got nothing to show for it.”

Hutt said the PAC’s endorsements have become a signal to the GOP establishment rather than the MAHA grassroots base.

“The telltale race that you did not see them get behind was the [Rep.] Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) race. If the PAC were going to stay true to their message and true to their support base, they would have come out strong in support of Thomas Massie,” Hutt said. “But the reluctance to do so or to get in on that campaign really showed to me that they’re promoting candidates that are aligned with the Trump White House.”

The MAHA movement is not a singular bloc, and there are different factions with priorities that don’t necessarily translate neatly into partisan camps. Some members prioritize changes to the food supply, some want tighter chemical and pesticide regulation, and some want to eliminate vaccine mandates.

MAHA activists have been growing increasing disillusioned with the Trump administration’s policies, and some prominent voices have been warning that when the November elections come around, MAHA voters may stay home.

“The [MAHA] endorsement itself won’t probably move the needle, but if they put a lot of money publicizing the endorsements, it could help GOP candidates some in tight races” Hutt said. “But either way, I think it will be minimal. If the GOP is hoping these endorsements are going to stem a blue wave, I’m afraid they are grasping at straws.”

articles.title: US Treasury's Bessent faces G20 diplomacy test amid tariffs, Iran war, bond turmoil
articles.summary: ASHEVILLE, North Carolina, Aug 30 (Reuters) - U. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent faces a major test of his economic diplomacy skills this week as he presses...
articles.body:
ASHEVILLE, North Carolina, Aug 30 (Reuters) - U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent faces a major test of his economic diplomacy skills this week as he presses finance leaders from the G20 major economies to shrink global trade imbalances, boost growth and sever business ties to Iran, while trying to calm worries about rising U.S. debt and bond yields.

After shunning the Group of 20 process last year ‌in South Africa, Bessent is seeking to revamp it under U.S. leadership to push the Trump administration's worldview in the Blue Ridge Mountains city of Asheville, North Carolina.

The meeting of finance ministers and central bank ‌governors on Monday and Tuesday comes at a time of massive uncertainty over the Trump administration's next tariff moves, its festering trade war with close ally Canada, and high energy and commodity prices due to the Iran war.

The unresolved conflict has kept the Strait of Hormuz closed, sapping growth from ​nearly all G20 economies. And Bessent has warned that countries face secondary U.S. sanctions if they continue to buy Iranian oil or facilitate other transactions with Tehran. On Friday he imposed curbs on a bank based in G20 member Egypt over links to Iran through its branches in the United Arab Emirates.

The combination of pressures adds up to potentially more discord in the widely diverse forum that includes China and Russia and has a hard time agreeing on any collective action while largely ignoring geopolitical tensions such as the war in Ukraine.

"Secretary Bessent will want to put Iran front and center and talk about tightening sanctions on Iran, and many countries around the G20 table will want to talk about anything else," said Josh Lipsky, international economics chair at ‌the Atlantic Council. "They'll want to talk about tariffs."

After the Supreme Court struck down ⁠President Donald Trump's broad global tariffs in February under a national emergencies law, his administration has been rebuilding the levies under different legal authorities.

All of the G20 countries and the European Union were among 60 economies hit in July with 10% or 12.5% U.S. tariffs for allegedly lax enforcement of forced labor bans. Sixteen top U.S. trading partners -- more than half of them ⁠G20 members -- are in line for more tariffs to counteract alleged excess industrial capacity under a separate trade probe.

The tariffs are central to the Trump administration's effort to reduce global trade imbalances, which a senior Treasury official said were the result of distortive government economic policies "that prevent fair competition" and that would be a major discussion topic at the Asheville meetings.

articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent began the week vowing an “economic onslaught” against Iran and its trading partners in a fresh bid to end the war. By the we...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent began the week vowing an "economic onslaught" against Iran and its trading partners in a fresh bid to end the war. By the week's end, countries with ties to Tehran had so far shrugged off the threat and analysts were left underwhelmed by the US actions.

China, which buys 90% of Iran's oil, issued a defiant warning to Washington rather than back down. Iranian bank branches remained open in Dubai. At one Bank Melli branch in Abu Dhabi, staff were busy typing away and one employee explained that they were still open for business.

Commercial flights also continued between Iran and Turkey as well as Iran and the United Arab Emirates, which had promised last week to sever all trade and financial transactions with Tehran. Routes flying to Thailand and Azerbaijan, as well as multiple destinations in both Russia and China, remained unaffected.

As the week came to a close, the US announced plans to sanction the UAE-based branches of Egypt's Banque Misr. That fell well below expectations after Bessent's warning that the world would see "a major announcement of a financial institution being sanctioned by the end of this week."

"As the war passes the six-month mark, the public actions taken by the Treasury Department this week do not match the hype," said Alex Zerden, a former US Treasury official and founder of Capitol Peak Strategies.

"Operation Economic Outcast is a continuation of 47 years of restrictive economic measures against Iran but does not provide a clearer theory of economic or military victory in this current campaign," Zerden said.

The Treasury Department didn't respond to a request for comment on Friday.

GLOBAL REACT: Trump's Iran 'D-Day' Hasn't Stormed Beaches

Bessent's threats — and the collective global shrug so far — underscore the Trump administration's main conundrum as it seeks to sanction Iran into meeting its demands. Any effective sanctions campaign would need to hit China, a move that risks sparking retaliation and potentially massive global economic fallout. Anything less would add to Iran's economic pain but not enough to budge its strategic calculus.

US credibility is also at stake. Bessent repeatedly compared the US response to the historic 1944 D-Day landings in Normandy, France — a coordinated land and air invasion aimed at toppling the Nazi regime. But the US acted unilaterally with its latest move, pressuring other countries rather than working with them, and Bessent openly acknowledged that going too fast and too hard risked tanking the global financial system.
authors: Yash Roy, Patrick Sykes and Alex Dooler

articles.title: Healthcare data breach exposes 3.75M patient records
articles.summary: The CareCloud data breach exposed Social Security numbers, banking information and medical records belonging to more than 3.75 million people.
articles.body: You can be careful with your passwords and still get caught in a breach at a company you may have never heard of. That is one of the frustrating parts of the CareCloud data breach. More than 3.75 million people had personal information and medical records stolen after hackers gained access to a CareCloud cloud environment earlier this year. CareCloud provides electronic medical record technology and other services to tens of thousands of healthcare providers across the U.S. So, even if you never created a CareCloud account, a doctor's office or another healthcare provider could have used its technology to handle your information. Now, we are getting a much clearer picture of just how much information hackers took. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com INSURANCE BREACH EXPOSES 7M DRIVER'S LICENSES CareCloud data breach affects more than 3.75 million people The cyberattack dates back to March 2026. According to a breach notice filed with the California Attorney General, CareCloud experienced a network disruption on March 16. The company brought in outside cybersecurity experts to investigate. CareCloud later determined that an unauthorized third party had access to one of its Amazon Web Services environments between March 10 and March 16, 2026. The company said the attacker claimed to have taken data from databases inside that environment. CareCloud also said it found no evidence of continued unauthorized activity after March 16. Early disclosures showed hundreds of thousands of people were affected. However, that figure later climbed dramatically. CareCloud has now reported that more than 3.75 million people were affected, according to federal health regulators. The disclosure places the incident among the largest healthcare data breaches reported so far in 2026. What hackers stole in the CareCloud data breach Here is where this breach becomes especially concerning. The stolen information goes well beyond an email address or phone number. What was exposed varies from person to person, but the data may include: Think about how much a criminal can learn from that combination. A Social Security number can help fuel identity theft. Banking information could put financial accounts at risk. Medical records can also give criminals deeply personal details that make phishing emails and scam calls far more convincing. Then there is another threat many people rarely think about: medical identity theft. MEDICAL IDENTITY THEFT FOLLOWS YOU INTO THE DOCTOR'S OFFICE Why stolen medical information can follow you for years You can change a password after a breach. Your medical history is much harder to replace. A criminal could use stolen insurance or personal information to seek medical care under someone else's identity. Fraudulent claims can also appear under a victim's health insurance. In some cases, incorrect treatment or medical information could eventually make its way into someone's records. That creates problems that can extend beyond financial fraud. The Federal Trade Commission advises people who suspect medical identity theft to review their medical records and insurance statements. Look closely for unfamiliar treatments, providers, prescriptions or charges. We recently covered this growing problem in Medical identity theft follows you into the doctor's office. What CareCloud says happened after the attack CareCloud says it brought in outside cybersecurity specialists after discovering the incident. The company also reported the attack to law enforcement and secured the affected environment. According to its breach notice, investigators found no continued unauthorized access after the incident was contained. CareCloud has also offered affected individuals complimentary identity protection services through IDX. If you received a notification letter, check it carefully for enrollment instructions and the amount of time you have to sign up. CyberGuy reached out to CareCloud for comment, but we did not hear back before our deadline. How to protect yourself after the CareCloud data breach A breach involving Social Security numbers, medical records and financial information deserves your attention even if you have not noticed anything suspicious yet. Here are the steps I recommend taking. 1) Read your CareCloud breach notice carefully Start with the letter or notification you received. Look for the specific types of information CareCloud says were involved in your case. Not every affected person necessarily had the same information exposed. If you were offered free identity protection or credit monitoring, review the terms and enrollment deadline. Consider signing up while the service remains available. 2) Freeze your credit If your Social Security number was exposed, consider freezing your credit with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A credit freeze limits access to your credit file. That can stop many criminals from opening new credit accounts in your name. Federal law allows you to freeze and unfreeze your credit for free. However, a credit freeze cannot block every form of identity theft. Someone could still attempt to take over an existing account or misuse your personal information in other ways. For a deeper look at those limitations, read Why a credit freeze isn't the end of identity theft. 3) Check your credit reports and financial accounts Keep an eye on your bank accounts, credit cards and credit reports. Look for purchases you do not recognize, unfamiliar credit inquiries or accounts you never opened. If something looks suspicious, contact the bank or financial institution directly. Use the phone number printed on your card or listed on the company's official website. Be wary of anyone who unexpectedly contacts you and claims they need personal information to investigate the CareCloud breach. 4) Review your medical records and insurance claims Do not limit your monitoring to your credit report. Sign in to your healthcare portals and review your records. Also look carefully at the explanation of benefits statements from your health insurer. Watch for unfamiliar doctors, procedures you never received or claims that make no sense. If something looks wrong, contact both your healthcare provider and insurer. Medical identity fraud may never trigger a traditional credit alert, which makes checking these records particularly important. 5) Protect your online accounts Use strong and unique passwords for important accounts, especially email, banking and healthcare services. If you reuse the same password on multiple sites, change it. A password manager can generate and securely store complex passwords so you do not have to remember them all. Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) whenever it is available. That extra verification step can make it harder for someone to get into an account even if they obtain your password. Pay extra attention to your primary email account. Criminals can use access to your inbox to reset passwords for other services. 6) Use strong antivirus software A stolen medical record could give a scammer enough personal information to send you a very convincing message. You might receive an email that appears to come from a doctor, health insurer or breach-response company. The message could include a malicious attachment or direct you to a fake login page. Strong antivirus software can help detect malicious links, dangerous downloads and other threats that arrive through phishing emails or scam messages. The best way to safeguard yourself from malicious links that install malware, potentially accessing your private information, is to have strong antivirus software installed on all your devices. This protection can also alert you to phishing emails and ransomware scams, helping keep your personal information and digital assets safer. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com 7) Watch closely for personalized scams This breach creates another problem. Scammers may now have enough real information about victims to sound believable. Be skeptical if someone suddenly contacts you claiming to represent CareCloud, your doctor, your insurance company or a credit-monitoring service. A criminal might know your name, address or other personal details. That knowledge does not make the person contacting you legitimate. Avoid clicking links in unexpected messages. Instead, open the organization's official website yourself or call a number you already trust. Also be suspicious of anyone demanding immediate payment or asking you to provide a verification code. 8) Use a personal data removal service The information stolen from CareCloud can become even more useful to criminals when they combine it with data that already appears online. People-search websites and data brokers can contain your phone number, current or previous addresses and other identifying information. Scammers can combine those details with breached data to build a more complete profile of you. A personal data removal service can help reduce your online footprint by sending removal requests to data brokers on your behalf. Some services also continue checking to see whether your information reappears. No service can guarantee that every piece of personal information will disappear from the internet. Still, removing information from data broker databases can make it harder for scammers to gather additional details about you. You can make removal requests yourself as well. However, doing it manually can be time-consuming and may require repeated requests. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com 9) Report identity theft quickly If you discover that someone is using your information, act quickly. Visit the Federal Trade Commission's IdentityTheft.gov website to report identity theft and create a personalized recovery plan. Keep records of suspicious transactions, emails and letters related to the fraud. Save copies of any reports you file as well. The sooner you spot suspicious activity, the sooner you can start limiting the damage. Kurt's key takeaways What bothers me most about the CareCloud breach is how little control you may have over where your medical information ends up. You can choose a doctor you trust. You can create strong passwords and protect your own devices. Yet some of your most sensitive information may still pass through another company's systems behind the scenes. That leaves millions of people dealing with the consequences when something goes wrong. If your information was involved, I would take the notification seriously even if everything looks normal today. A stolen Social Security number or medical record can remain useful to criminals long after the original breach fades from the news. Freeze your credit if your Social Security number was exposed. Watch your medical records and financial accounts over time. Then be especially cautious when an unexpected email, call or text seems to know surprisingly personal details about you. I would also reduce what data brokers can easily find about you and keep strong antivirus protection running on your devices. Those added layers can make follow-up attacks harder for scammers to pull off. articles.title: Google Maps to change Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’ on US phones
articles.summary: Google Maps on Saturday changed the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” for U.S. users, while keeping the name intact for Canadian Google users and carrying both names for international users, following President Trump’s executive order to rename the Great Lake. The tech giant cited its name change to the U.S. Geographic Names Information…
articles.body:
Google Maps on Saturday changed the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” for U.S. users, while keeping the name intact for Canadian Google users and carrying both names for international users, following President Trump’s executive order to rename the Great Lake.

The tech giant cited its name change to the U.S. Geographic Names Information System’s (GNIS) formal renaming.

“Since we update Google Maps to reflect name changes in official government sources, which is GNIS for the U.S., people using Maps in the U.S. will see ‘Lake America,’ those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario,’ and those outside of the U.S. and Canada will see both names,” the company said in a statement .

Trump signed an executive order to rename the Great Lake, “ effective immediately ,” amid his trade war with Canada, which has retaliated with its own tariffs on copper wire, wood, charcoal, steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics, leaving seafood and fish products exempt.

He cited the lake’s natural resources and historical ties to the U.S.’s early development to recognize this “flourishing economic resource and its critical importance to our Nation’s economy and its people.”

Google’s move to rename the lake resembles its renaming of the Gulf of Mexico last year, after Trump signed an executive order to rename it the “Gulf of America.”

That order stated that the label applies to “the U.S. Continental Shelf area bounded on the northeast, north, and northwest by the States of Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama and Florida and extending to the seaward boundary with Mexico and Cuba in the area formerly named as the Gulf of Mexico.”

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said in February 2025 that the name change affected “the continental shelf of Mexico and Cuba, which has nothing to do with Trump’s decree, which applied only to the U.S. continental shelf.”

The Mexican government later sued Google in May 2025.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford on Sunday said the Great Lake’s renaming was “like something out of ‘Saturday Night Live .'”

“No one’s going to call it Lake America,” Ford told “This Week” host Martha Raddatz on ABC. “It’s been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It’s going to continue to be Lake Ontario.”

The Seneca Nation, one of the six nations of the Haudenosaunee, or Iroquois, Confederacy, on Friday called on Trump to rescind the order , with President J. Conrad Seneca saying the renaming violated the terms of the 1794 Treaty of Canandaigua .

The treaty, signed by Haudenosaunee leaders and President George Washington, laid out the Seneca Nation’s boundaries as “beginning on Lake Ontario.” In Seneca, the body of water is called “sga:nyodai:yoh,” which translates to “beautiful lake.”

“The President cannot assert ownership over our culture or erase it through irresponsible political action,” Seneca said in a statement.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney also denounced the name change , pointing to the Wendat Nation’s word to describe the lake, Ontari’io, “which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.”

articles.title: Homan pushes back on alleged ICE arrests of parents at bus stops
articles.summary: White House border czar Tom Homan on Sunday pushed back on the idea of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arresting parents at bus stops in Connecticut, as alleged by Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) this week. “I pointed out, the last two years, no one can point to one single incidence we arrested anybody in elementary…
articles.body:
White House border czar Tom Homan on Sunday pushed back on the idea of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arresting parents at bus stops in Connecticut, as alleged by Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) this week.

“I pointed out, the last two years, no one can point to one single incidence we arrested anybody in elementary school. We haven’t arrested anybody in the hospital. We haven’t arrested anybody in the church. ICE is real good at their job,” Homan told CNN’s Dana Bash on “State of the Union.”

“Now, did they arrest somebody at a bus stop? I’m not aware of that, but ICE is out there to enforce law against those that have been ordered removed by a federal judge. And especially if they’re a criminal or if they’re a national security threat, there’s no safe harbor for them in this country,” he added.

Earlier this week, Murphy wrote on social media that “ICE was arresting parents at school bus stops” in Danbury, Conn.

“But it’s more sinister. ICE waited until the kids were on the bus so when they are dropped off at the end of the day, they are alone, scared to death they can’t find their parents. I’m heading to Danbury,” the senator added in his Wednesday post.

Throughout President Trump’s second term in office, his administration has faced backlash over its strict immigration agenda. That backlash boiled over earlier this year when two U.S. citizens were killed in Minneapolis by federal immigration authorities, and since then, more people have been killed in confrontations with immigration enforcement in other states including Maine and Texas.

Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont (D) wrote in his own social media post on Thursday that he was “horrified by the stories shared by activists in Danbury.”

“Parents detained dropping their children off at the school bus. 3 year old children watching ICE forcibly detain someone outside their daycare window. Rounding up people at random to meet a quota doesn’t make our communities safer,” he added.

articles.title: Sunrises before 5 a.m.? How permanent standard time would impact summer mornings
articles.summary: Summer mornings could feel a lot different if we stopped observing daylight saving time during part of the year.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – While it’s permanent daylight saving time that the U.S. is closest to adopting, there remains a bill in Congress that could lock the clocks on standard time.

As of late August, the Sunshine for Our Kids Act of 2026 remains in the House Committee on Energy and Commerce. If it were to be enacted into law in its current form, standard time would become permanent , but states would be allowed to make daylight saving time permanent (states can only opt to observe year-round standard time at present).

Several health experts have spoken out in favor of permanent standard time due to the benefits it could have on our overall well-being . But opponents have pointed to how the move would alter summer sunsets .

Standard time is the time we observe from early November until early March. That would mean our clocks would not fall back an hour in March, causing our spring, summer, and early fall sunrises and sunsets to slide forward an hour.

For many, that would mean summer sunsets before 8 p.m. In some areas, the summer sun would set earlier than 7 p.m.

Permanent standard time would, of course, also impact our summer sunrises.

Across June, July, and August – what we’re broadly defining as “summer” – the earliest sunrises in the U.S. at present range between around 5 a.m. and 6:30 a.m. If standard time were to become permanent, those times would shift to 4 a.m. to 5:30 a.m.

In Green Bay, Wisconsin, for example, the earliest sunrise the city sees during the summer is 5:07 a.m. Under permanent standard time, that would become 4:07 a.m. For 79 of the 92 summer days we analyzed, the sun would rise before 5 a.m. in Green Bay.

The interactive table below shows how summer sunrises would change across 33 cities under permanent standard time. On the far right side, you can see the earliest summer sunrises these cities currently experience, and what that time would become under permanent standard time.

Omitted from the table but potentially the most impacted is Alaska. In Juneau, there would be 48 sunrises before 4 a.m. through June and early July. Only 20 of the 92 sunrise times reviewed by Nexstar would happen after 5 a.m. Juneau’s earliest summer sunrise would happen at 3:20 a.m.

The table also doesn’t consider the states that have enacted permanent daylight saving time legislation already , making them likely to pursue the same plan if the Sunshine for Our Kids Act were to pass.

As strange as it may be to wake up to such early sunrises during the summer, health experts have argued that it is likely what your body prefers . Having more sunlight exposure in the morning is crucial for our melatonin system, Dr. Alaina Tiani, a clinical health psychologist who specializes in behavioral sleep medicine at the Cleveland Clinic’s Sleep Disorder Center, previously told Nexstar. It can also prove beneficial for our circadian rhythm.

“When our circadian rhythms are working well, they help us anticipate our day,” Dr. Karin Johnson, spokesperson for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) and co-chair of the Coalition for Permanent Standard Time , said during a Senate hearing on daylight saving time last year .

On hotter summer days, observing standard time may also offer an advantage that most of one state is already taking advantage of : earlier reprieve from the hot sun. A contributing factor for Arizona’s decision to lock its clocks on permanent standard time is that the sun will set earlier in the day, helping those sweltering hot days not feel so long.

It’s difficult to say whether the Sunshine for Our Kids Act will pass out of the House committee it’s in. The House already passed the Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time permanent in the U.S. That bill is now in the Senate, where it faces an uncertain future, despite support from President Trump .

Regardless of whether you ( or your lawmakers ) prefer permanent daylight saving time or permanent standard time, the study – published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences – determined that changing the clocks twice a year is the worst of the three options.

Without any quick action in Congress, clocks will “fall back” an hour on the earliest possible date this year.

articles.body: BENGALURU: A 23-year-old software engineer died while her 30-year-old lover sustained serious injuries after the two allegedly jumped from the seventh-floor terrace of a co-living paying guest accommodation in Whitefield on Sunday afternoon.The deceased, identified as Janani, worked as a software engineer with a financial services company in Pattanduru Agrahara near Whitefield. He is undergoing treatment at Vydehi Institute of Medical Sciences and Research Centre in Whitefield and is reportedly out of danger.“Once Velu is in a condition to give his statement, we will question him and know further details about their extreme step,” a senior officer said.Janani had earlier been staying at another PG in the same area. “We suspect that they both lived in the same room,” the officer added.Velu works for a logistics company in Puducherry. articles.title: Senate Democrat says Ukraine needs ‘more air defense’
articles.summary: Rep. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) said Ukraine requires “more air defense” in its war against Russia. “[Russian President Vladimir] Putin is a mob thug. He understands only force and strength. And so, to send the CIA director, as President Biden did, Director Burns, to warn or try to persuade Putin with words, actions speak louder than…
articles.body:
Rep. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) said Ukraine requires “more air defense” in its war against Russia.

“[Russian President Vladimir] Putin is a mob thug. He understands only force and strength. And so, to send the CIA director, as President Biden did, Director Burns, to warn or try to persuade Putin with words, actions speak louder than words, largely going to be ineffective,” Blumenthal told CBS News’s Margaret Brennan on “Face the Nation,” discussing a recent trip to Russia by CIA Director John Ratcliffe.

“And the Europeans understand that right now, what’s needed is more air defense,” he added.

According to multiple reports, a surprise trip to Moscow by Ratcliffe served to advise Russia against attacking NATO countries. President Trump called the CIA director’s visit “semi-routine” on Wednesday and Baltic officials played down any threat of an attack in the near future.

The happenings of Ratcliffe’s meeting were first reported on by The Wall Street Journal. The most recent trip to Russia by the CIA director happened in late 2021, when Bill Burns went to warn Putin against launching his full-scale invasion into Ukraine.

Ratcliffe’s recent meeting came alongside Russia intensifying its aerial attacks against Ukraine and a rising number of civilians being killed.

Per earlier reporting from the Journal, the U.S. intelligence community assessed the Russian president could attempt to test NATO’s strength via a limited assault on an allied country in the coming years.

The Hill was told by a European official that the U.S. briefed allies about Ratcliffe’s trip and that it centered around Ukraine. According to the official, there was no imminent military threat to NATO.

articles.title: Airlines for America CEO says plane ticket prices will stabilize
articles.summary: Airlines for America CEO Chris Sununu on Sunday said the price of plane tickets will stabilize amid high jet fuel prices that have spiked in the six months since the Iran war began. “People realize that demand is high,” Sununu told “The Hill Sunday” host Chris Stirewalt on NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network. “I don’t…
articles.body:
Airlines for America CEO Chris Sununu on Sunday said the price of plane tickets will stabilize amid high jet fuel prices that have spiked in the six months since the Iran war began.

“People realize that demand is high,” Sununu told “The Hill Sunday” host Chris Stirewalt on NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network. “I don’t think you’re going to see prices go up significantly. I think they’re going to be kind of stabilized for quite a while because we’re not getting out of this Iran thing anytime soon, unfortunately. And it’s a bigger issue for places like Asia and Europe.”

The average price of jet fuel is $3.82, down from $4 back in May. Domestic and international prices peaked the same month, with flights within the U.S. close to $100 more than they were for domestic flights last year and international flights costing more than $200 more compared to last year, according to Kayak.

Sununu said that the price for domestic flights is up 20 percent, adding that he does not “think it’s going up anymore.”

“Demand is strong. People are traveling,” he said. “And that puts money in the economy in a whole lot of different ways. So overall, it’s a very good thing economically.”

Even with high demand, the former New Hampshire governor said that the price of jet fuel has more than doubled and airlines “are eating the cost.”

“So that is up 20 percent, but it really should almost double if they passed all the cost to the consumers,” he continued. “They’re not doing that. So they’re staying competitive.”

Airlines have seen jet fuel prices soar and nearly double in some cases. United and American Airlines both estimated about $6 billion increases in fuel costs compared to last year, both 50 percent jumps from 2025, according to CNBC .

The Bureau of Transportation Statistics found in July that the price increase was driven mostly by the rising cost of fuel rather than demand, with airlines consuming 1.627 billion gallons in May, while the average price paid nearly doubled from where it was in May 2025, reaching $4.09 per gallon.

Fuel is one of the industry’s biggest operating expenses, with high costs forcing carriers to raise fares and cut flights. Spirit Airlines, after failing to receive a bailout from the Trump administration, shut down in May as a result of high fuel prices.

The U.S. has maintained a naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz, where roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil is exported. Iran has kept the strait closed, seeking deals with other countries in the region, such as Oman, for routes through which oil can be exported.

articles.title: Freedom Fuel gas stations sold stolen fuel, lawsuit claims
articles.summary: Freedom Fuel gas stations, which the Trump administration promoted last month, sold fuel that its supplier never paid for, according to a lawsuit filed earlier this month. The suit, which attorneys for Mansfield Oil Company filed in U.S. District Court in Eastern Pennsylvania on Aug. 19, alleges that KRSM, a foreign corporation, obtained in excess…
articles.body:
Freedom Fuel gas stations, which the Trump administration promoted last month , sold fuel that its supplier never paid for, according to a lawsuit filed earlier this month.

The suit , which attorneys for Mansfield Oil Company filed in U.S. District Court in Eastern Pennsylvania on Aug. 19, alleges that KRSM, a foreign corporation, obtained in excess of 1.1 million gallons of fuel from the former company’s account from May 21 through July 7.

The fuel cost nearly $4 million, the 179-page lawsuit states. But as of Aug. 17, KRSM had not paid for the fuel, despite Mansfield, a foreign corporation with offices in Gainesville, Ga., sending revised invoices to the defendant on July 17.

While the agreement between the two companies stipulated that KRSM had to pay the invoices within 10 days of receiving them, Mansfield’s bank advised on July 28 that the foreign firm had “refused” draft requests, the lawsuit stated.

Of the roughly 1.1 million gallons of fuel KRSM obtained from Mansfield, it sold “a portion” of it to stations in the Freedom Fuel Network, per the suit.

Last month, President Trump touted 25 gas stations within the network, highlighting their lower prices relative to the national average. Amid the Iran war, the national average price of a gallon of regular gas is roughly $4.07 as of Sunday, per data from AAA .

A White House official told The Hill in July the network is a private company and has not received federal funding. The network now has 29 locations, with all located in New Jersey or Pennsylvania, according to its website .

Trump said on July 1 the network’s stations were “taking the lead” on lowering gas prices and urged other retailers to follow suit.

White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers echoed those remarks, telling The Hill last month the Freedom Fuel stations “are doing their part to answer the President’s call to lower prices at the pump.”

But the lawsuit brought by Mansfield alleges KRSM was able to sell fuel to Freedom Fuel at discounted prices and “garner such publicity” because it “never paid” the plaintiff for it.

The Hill has reached out to the Freedom Fuel Network and the White House for comment on the allegations in the suit.

KRSM is led by Syed Kazmi, who signed Mansfield’s commercial credit application in January 2022, as shown by a copy included in the lawsuit.

Under that application, Kazmi agreed that if Mansfield extended credit to KRSM and his company purchased fuel from the creditor, KRSM would be “responsible” to pay for it.
